title: Dacarbazine — metastatic melanoma
purpose: To control metastatic melanoma with chemotherapy, with benefit, blood counts and tolerability reviewed before each treatment.

agents.name: Dacarbazine
agents.explanation: Dacarbazine is converted in the body into substances that damage DNA and make it harder for cancer cells to divide. It also affects some healthy cells, including blood-forming cells. This explains why nausea prevention and blood-count checks are central to the plan.
agents.watch: Report fever or feeling acutely unwell, bleeding, persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain or burning at the infusion site.
risks: Low white cells, platelets or red cells
Rare severe liver injury or allergic reaction

passport_visit_note: Record the dose actually taken or administered, symptoms, tests and agreed next step. A planned or held visit is not a completed treatment dose.
anatomy: Tiredness, anaemia, poor sleep and nausea can affect concentration. Report severe dizziness, confusion or a major change in function; do not drive if unwell.
Low white cells increase infection risk and may occur late in the cycle. Fever or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent contact, even near the next planned dose.
Low red cells can cause tiredness or breathlessness. New or worsening breathlessness needs assessment; severe breathlessness or chest pain is an emergency.
Hair loss or sun sensitivity can occur. New severe rash, swelling or breathing difficulty may indicate allergy and needs urgent help.
Rare severe liver injury can cause abdominal pain, fever and jaundice. Seek urgent assessment; routine liver tests do not replace symptom reporting.
Vomiting and reduced intake can lead to dehydration. Report reduced urine, persistent vomiting or inability to drink; kidney tests also help guide dosing.
Nausea and vomiting need preventive medicines and a take-home plan. Report persistent symptoms, severe abdominal pain or failure of rescue treatment.
Pain, burning, swelling or redness during infusion can mean leakage outside the vein. Tell the nurse immediately because tissue injury is possible.
Low platelets can cause bruising, nosebleeds or bleeding gums. Persistent bleeding, black stools or blood in urine require prompt assessment.

chronology_notes.title: Schedule and review
chronology_notes.text: Dacarbazine by IV infusion on day 1, repeated every 21 days for up to six cycles, or stopped earlier for progression or unacceptable toxicity.

chronology_notes.title: Holds, missed treatment and phase changes
chronology_notes.text: If treatment is delayed for low blood counts, illness or another problem, the team sets the new date and dose. Do not mark a planned but cancelled dose as received. The six-cycle limit is conditional on benefit and tolerability, not a requirement to give unsafe treatment.

administration_text: The NCCP dose is dacarbazine 850 mg/m² on day 1 in one litre of saline over one hour, with the infusion protected from light. The individual dose is prescribed using body size and clinical review. Allow extra time for blood results, anti-sickness medicine, preparation and any other fluids. Tell the nurse immediately about pain, burning, swelling or redness around the infusion.
monitoring_summary: Full blood count, kidney and liver function, medicines and prior treatment history. Discuss pregnancy prevention and fertility before the first dose. Record symptoms and the disease sites being followed on scans. Full blood count, kidney and liver function before every cycle. Blood-count suppression can be delayed: the product information describes the lowest counts often three to four weeks after a dose, so a 21-day appointment does not guarantee recovery. Extra blood tests are arranged when clinically needed. Keep reporting fever, bleeding, worsening fatigue or other symptoms after the last infusion while counts and organs recover. Response scans, later blood tests and the next treatment decision are individual; the NCCP source gives no universal imaging or tumour-marker schedule.

support.title: Supportive medicines and symptom plan
support.text: Dacarbazine has high nausea-and-vomiting risk, so a planned preventive anti-sickness regimen is needed under the local protocol, including clear take-home instructions. The NCCP line that routine premedication is usually unnecessary does not remove this antiemetic requirement. Ask what to take regularly, what is rescue treatment and when to call if it fails.

support.title: Skin and daily care
support.text: Hair loss and sun sensitivity can occur, though they are not inevitable. Use gentle skin care and sun protection. Report redness, pain or swelling at a previous infusion site, or a spreading rash or signs of an allergic reaction.

support.title: Fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding
support.text: The current HPRA product information advises effective contraception during treatment and for six months after the final dose for women, and during treatment and for three months afterwards for men. Discuss fertility preservation and, when relevant, genetic counselling before treatment. Do not breastfeed during treatment; ask the team about the appropriate interval afterwards.

evidence.title: What the treatment evidence can and cannot tell you
evidence.intro: Evidence needs to match the medicine, dose combination, disease stage and previous treatment.
evidence.population: 418 previously untreated patients with metastatic BRAF-wild-type melanoma
evidence.interpretation: The dacarbazine comparator response rate was 13.9%; this is not a validated efficacy estimate for NCCP dacarbazine 850 mg/m². These are group results from that study, not a prediction for you.
limitations: Dacarbazine dose differs from NCCP 00464, and the population was BRAF wild type.
The study primarily established benefit of nivolumab over a historical comparator.
No exact survival or response prediction is assigned to the NCCP 850 mg/m² course.
Personal benefit depends on the cancer, previous treatment, general health and the available alternatives.

chapters.title: Understanding your diagnosis and treatment goal
chapters.intro: Use your own pathology, stage and agreed plan alongside this guide.

items.title: Your diagnosis and stage
items.text: Keep the pathology report, original melanoma site, stage and known sites of spread. This guide concerns advanced disease that cannot be removed completely by surgery or has spread; it does not describe a postoperative recurrence-prevention course.

items.title: The tumour test
items.text: A BRAF V600 test helps identify whether BRAF-targeted medicines are an option. A tumour mutation does not by itself mean an inherited family condition. Keep the exact result and ask how it changes your choices.

items.title: Scans and local treatments
items.text: Record the scans used to follow known disease. Surgery or radiotherapy may have a separate role for a particular site; ask for their timing and risks to be added to the overall plan.

items.title: New changes still matter
items.text: Report a new lump, changing mole, persistent skin sore or unexplained symptom. A response at one site does not establish that every other symptom is harmless.

items.title: Other medicines
items.text: Give the team a complete list of prescribed, over-the-counter and herbal medicines, supplements and allergies. Ask before adding a new medicine; treatment interactions and symptom-masking can matter.

items.title: Practical arrangements
items.text: Know where and when bloods are taken, how results reach the prescriber, and how to obtain the next supply or appointment. Ask for written instructions in a format you can use without a phone.

chapters.title: Tests, results and treatment decisions
chapters.intro: Safety tests and scans answer different questions.

items.title: Before treatment
items.text: Full blood count, kidney and liver function, medicines and prior treatment history. Discuss pregnancy prevention and fertility before the first dose. Record symptoms and the disease sites being followed on scans.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: Full blood count, kidney and liver function before every cycle. Extra blood tests are arranged when clinically needed.

items.title: What a result means
items.text: Ask which result is abnormal, whether the finding needs a repeat test and whether treatment is held, changed or stopped. Do not use a reference range or one normal result to decide independently that a dose is safe.

items.title: Response and follow-up
items.text: Keep reporting fever, bleeding, worsening fatigue or other symptoms after the last infusion while counts and organs recover. Response scans, later blood tests and the next treatment decision are individual; the NCCP source gives no universal imaging or tumour-marker schedule.

chapters.title: What to expect between visits
chapters.intro: A quiet treatment day does not rule out later problems.

items.title: Act on new symptoms
items.text: Follow your unit’s fever threshold and urgent-contact instructions; call immediately if you develop fever, shaking chills or feel suddenly unwell, even without a high temperature. items.title: A useful daily record
items.text: Record symptoms, temperature when unwell, bowel changes, fluid intake when reduced, missed doses and any medicines used for relief. Note how symptoms affect eating, walking, sleep and normal activities; this helps the team judge severity.

items.title: When life is affected
items.text: Tell the team about fatigue, pain, appetite, sleep, mood and ability to work or care for others. Practical and supportive care can accompany anticancer treatment; you do not have to wait until treatment ends.

chapters.title: Skin, body changes and daily care
chapters.intro: Use the detailed body map to locate symptoms, not to diagnose them.

items.title: Skin and sun
items.text: Hair loss and sun sensitivity can occur, though they are not inevitable. Use gentle skin care and sun protection. Report redness, pain or swelling at a previous infusion site, or a spreading rash or signs of an allergic reaction.

items.title: The body map
items.text: The organ anchors show possible locations and warning symptoms. They do not show how common each effect is, and a symptom may have another cause. New symptoms should be assessed in their clinical context.

items.title: Food, fluids and activity
items.text: Keep meals and fluids manageable and follow any individual fluid or diet restrictions. Gentle activity and rest can be adjusted to how you feel. Ask for dietetic or rehabilitation help if intake, weight, strength or mobility is falling.

items.title: Keep checking the plan
items.text: A new medicine, fever, hospital admission, procedure or radiotherapy may change treatment timing. Tell the oncology team and take the wallet card or medicine list to other appointments.

chapters.title: Fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding
chapters.intro: Discuss these issues before the first dose whenever possible.

items.title: Contraception and pregnancy
items.text: The current HPRA product information advises effective contraception during treatment and for six months after the final dose for women, and during treatment and for three months afterwards for men. Discuss fertility preservation and, when relevant, genetic counselling before treatment. Do not breastfeed during treatment; ask the team about the appropriate interval afterwards.

items.title: Fertility preservation
items.text: Ask whether treatment or the cancer may affect fertility and whether fertility preservation is appropriate before treatment. A change in periods or sexual function does not reliably establish infertility.

items.title: Written dates and methods
items.text: Record the agreed method, last treatment date and how long precautions continue. Different medicines have different intervals, so ask for clarification after a switch or combination change.

items.title: Sexual health
items.text: Tell the team about sexual symptoms, relationship concerns or practical difficulties with the agreed precautions. Ask for a private discussion and specialist support when needed.

chapters.title: Decisions, support and useful records
chapters.intro: Your priorities belong in the treatment discussion.

items.title: Benefits and alternatives
items.text: Ask what the treatment aims to achieve, what alternatives are suitable, how likely important benefits are in your situation and how treatment burden or uncertainty affects that choice. A trial average cannot promise an individual outcome.

items.title: Support alongside treatment
items.text: Ask about symptom control, psychological support, finances, transport, work and help at home. Palliative or supportive care can be used alongside anticancer treatment to improve comfort and function.

items.title: A person you trust
items.text: If helpful, bring a family member or supporter and agree what information may be shared. Ask for an interpreter or accessible information when needed; use teach-back to check the schedule and urgent plan.

items.title: Your document set
items.text: Keep consent information, the three-page summary, complete handbook, treatment card, test plan and real contact details together. The QR opens more information but essential instructions remain available in print.

chapters.title: After a treatment hold, change or completion
chapters.intro: The next step should be written down, not assumed.

items.title: Follow-up and late effects
items.text: Keep reporting fever, bleeding, worsening fatigue or other symptoms after the last infusion while counts and organs recover. Response scans, later blood tests and the next treatment decision are individual; the NCCP source gives no universal imaging or tumour-marker schedule.

items.title: Restarting or changing treatment
items.text: If treatment is delayed for low blood counts, illness or another problem, the team sets the new date and dose. Do not mark a planned but cancelled dose as received. The six-cycle limit is conditional on benefit and tolerability, not a requirement to give unsafe treatment.

items.title: A treatment summary
items.text: Record medicines and doses received, important side effects, admissions, last-dose date, ongoing symptom treatment and the clinician responsible for follow-up. Ask for an updated paper copy for your GP and other treating teams.

items.title: Your next review
items.text: Confirm the next blood test, scan and review, who explains the result, and which symptoms should trigger contact sooner. Keep actual daytime and out-of-hours numbers accessible after treatment stops.
